title: Analytical data dictionary
text: This dictionary documents the data used in the recruitment study: paired forest conditions, recorded sapling entry, model predictors, and linked sapling fates. Record-level data and predictions remain local; public outputs contain aggregate evidence.

title: Analytical data dictionary

Analytical units and keys
The primary analytical unit is one forest condition observed across two linked visits. A physical plot can contain multiple conditions. Tree and seedling summaries join to the condition pair at the appropriate level to avoid multiplying observations through many-to-many joins.
data/processed/recruitment_condition_pairs.rds retains 932 source pairs, including excluded observations. Of these, 922 qualify for analysis, representing 903 physical plots and 66 counties. The source spans baseline measurements in 2011–2018 and follow-ups in 2018–2025.

title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
Recruitment endpoint
A qualifying new live sugar-maple sapling has SPCD=318, STATUSCD=1, diameter at least 1 inch and less than 5 inches, RECONCILECD=1, and no predecessor TREE record. It must occur on a comparable shared sampled microplot.








Field
Type / unit
Definition




new_maple_sapling_count
Count
Qualifying new live maple sapling records assigned to the condition pair; interpretation requires recruitment_eligible.


ambiguous_new_maple_sapling_count
Count
Newly recorded live maple saplings that lack a resolved entrant classification; positive values prevent recruitment eligibility.


outcome_recruitment
0 / 1 / NA
At least one qualifying entrant on an eligible interval; excluded intervals retain NA.


followup_zero_tree_corrected
Logical
Explicit correction of derived tree quantities for a source-verified sampled follow-up with no live TREE records and BALIVE=0.



The retained cohort contains 169 qualifying saplings in 100 conditions. These records describe surviving entrants present at the next visit. They do not link individual baseline seedlings to later trees or identify entrants that died before remeasurement.
The endpoint definitions and protocol audit document the rules. Implementation: R/recruitment.R.

Four logistic models use training prevalence, design variables, design plus count, and design plus count plus maple stages. Each model uses its declared subset of the five predictors. All eligible intervals and the 672 intervals with positive baseline counts have separately fitted comparisons.
Training means and standard deviations determine scaling of both training and held-out observations. A constant training predictor uses a scale of one. Bootstrap fits repeat this process. The primary ridge penalty equals one and leaves the intercept unpenalized.
Ordinary counts may include field estimates above five seedlings per record. TPA_UNADJ expands observations within the plot design and is not a statewide survey weight. Neither raw count nor seedling density identifies independent seed-origin individuals.
Implementation: R/recruitment_models.R.

title: Analytical data dictionary
text:
Geographic and interpretation boundaries
The study map counts eligible recruitment intervals by geoid. Its colors describe sample coverage. The analysis does not use or infer exact FIA plot coordinates or estimate county regeneration rates.
The outcomes and scores are descriptive or predictive results for the selected Michigan sample. They do not provide survey-weighted population estimates, individual seedling survival, a causal effect, or an operational treatment rule.
See Analysis decisions for the cohort and comparison rules and the research paper for their results.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
This optional follow-up plan specifies how a future study could evaluate the field usefulness of regeneration measurements. It builds on the completed Michigan recruitment study.
Determine whether additional regeneration measurements improve a specified survey decision enough to justify their collection cost, compared with a simple seedling-count rule. The existing recruitment models do not yet demonstrate such an advantage. This plan defines a possible subsequent study; no new survey, external validation, or operational deployment has occurred.
The current survey-priority comparison uses no new sapling recorded at follow-up as a diagnostic target. It is not independently assessed survey need. At 25% capacity among 672 baseline-detected conditions, low counts identify an expected 162 no-entry conditions, the count model 160, and the stage model 163. The one-condition stage gain is uncertain and is not reproduced in the later-year test using realized intervals.

title: Survey validation plan
section: Completed measurement milestone and remaining limits
text:
Completed measurement milestone and remaining limits
The local audit has produced an eligibility flow, code/measurement reconciliation, and descriptive support tables. The checklist below records its required components; historical annual-guide coverage remains qualified, and it does not authorize a new model:

Resolve historical RI length-class and source-code definitions from the applicable guides. Standard hardwood minimum length and FIA sapling DBH boundaries are not interchangeable with RI height classes.
Verify REGEN_MICR_STATUS_CD, older subplot-status fields, condition coverage, dates, and sampled microplots at the baseline used for recruitment prediction. Missing status and absent species records require explicit rules.
Reconcile total RI counts, length classes, vegetative-origin categories, and ordinary seedling tallies without forcing agreement across different minimum-size definitions. Do not include the browse-impact score as an independent cause without checking whether regeneration scarcity enters it.
Publish an eligibility flow and event/plot support. Use the same conditions for simple-count and height-information comparisons; do not compare metrics from different populations as if only the predictor changed.
Assess precision and model complexity before fitting. If the audited subset remains too weak for the proposed comparison, report the descriptive measurement audit and stop. Do not fill the gap with an optimistic model.

The descriptive result is 13 recruit-bearing conditions among 44 with baseline maple at least five feet long, versus one among 46 without. A later-year split would have ten development events and four assessment events. That does not support a strong claim about incremental forecasting value. The next study must evaluate length information against ordinary counts on a better-supported, separate sample, with a meaningful target and gain specified before evaluation.
Height information is a grounded candidate: the regional FIA study by Harris, Woodall, and D’Amato (2022) found better recruitment models with height classes than with ordinary combined counts. That precedent motivates the measurement comparison; it does not prove the Michigan subset is adequate or that a field survey would be cost-effective.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Requirements for an operational study
The count-versus-length design now specifies the research comparison and executable precision scenarios. Its historical Michigan metadata census finds 88 positive-seedling opportunities on 79 plots before full eligibility checks, only six plots outside the current recruitment cohort. These are not new event counts or an independent evaluation set. The project includes a Wisconsin/Minnesota feasibility screen, not model fitting on those rows. Archive access currently blocks that screen, so the regional work remains a feasibility plan rather than a result. The conditional next-visit research target remains distinct from the operational requirements below.
Before describing a ranking as a survey tool, the following must be specified with the intended decision owner. These choices are not supplied by the current database analysis.







Requirement
Why it matters




Management or research question
Locating low advancement, locating successful recruits, estimating prevalence, and learning mechanisms require different sampling strategies.


Independently assessed target
No recorded entry is not automatically a stocking deficit, survey need, or treatable problem. Specify the field criterion and horizon without using the prediction to define the answer.


Unit of action
A management stand or physical visit is not a FIA condition interval. Define eligibility and cost at the actual sampling unit.


Measurements and timing
Specify repeatable size/height, vigor, stocking, and damage observations and the forecasting date. Use a planned horizon rather than a realized future interval.


Cost and error consequences
Travel, access, measurement time, missed problem sites, and unnecessary visits determine whether an incremental gain matters. There is no universal 25% budget.


Separate evaluation sample
Reserve locations, inventory periods, or a prospective sample before choosing models and cutoffs. Shared plots must not cross development and evaluation.



Accuracy metrics alone do not establish value. Decision-analytic methods relate predictions to meaningful error consequences; a threshold chosen solely to make a model look good is not such a preference. Vickers and Elkin (2006) provide the general methodological rationale, not forestry utilities or a recommended decision threshold for this project.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Evaluation design
Keep low raw count and count per sampled coverage as fixed comparators. Declare which direction is useful for the independent target. If height data are evaluated, add only the scientifically motivated, supportable representation selected before observing evaluation outcomes; tune within development data.
Measure the target on a probability-based evaluation sample or a design with known selection probabilities. Assessing only model-selected sites cannot reveal missed sites or provide an unbiased model-versus-simple-rule comparison. Retain a random or stratified component across score levels, and document nonresponse and inaccessible sites. Exact FIA locations are not inferred.
Compare selected-target yield, missed-target fraction, calibration where probabilities are relevant, and actual cost per useful finding at matched plot/stand-level capacity. Use clustered uncertainty appropriate to the new sample and analyze predefined target subgroups. Report ties and protocol changes. A held-out later inventory on a known plot is a different assessment from transfer to a new location.
Choose sample size through a precision/power assessment for the paired gain that would change the decision, using realistic target frequency and within-site dependence. Do not claim adequacy from a fixed events-per-variable rule. The current 14 RI-overlap events are a feasibility warning, not a sample-size plan.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Decision gates
Proceed to a field-facing tool only if the measurement audit passes, a real decision is specified, and the separate evaluation shows a useful improvement over the simple benchmark after accounting for collection cost and uncertainty. Failure to demonstrate an improvement is an informative result; retain the simple strategy or conclude that the target needs better measurement.
The separate scope decision now authorizes Wisconsin/Minnesota inventory acquisition and feasibility screening. It does not authorize field coordination, fieldwork, or further geography changes. The baseline measurement audit is complete with the stated historical-access qualification. The 14-event subset should not be promoted into a larger fitted model or a management claim.

title: Survey validation plan
text:
Reproducibility
Run make survey-audit after the recruitment model bundle exists. Script 16 reproduces the capacity comparison and full-refit uncertainty; script 17 reproduces the RI availability screen. The separate make ri-audit target reproduces the measurement and support audit. The analysis decisions and reproducibility guide separate declared choices, local results, and external evidence.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
The Michigan regeneration-indicator (RI) records support a descriptive measurement study, but not a strong new forecasting claim. The baseline sampling and record checks retain 90 condition intervals on 87 physical plots, with 14 recruit-bearing conditions. The audit examines whether seedling length measurements add distinct information beyond the ordinary counts recorded on the same sampled area.
Taller seedlings provide a plausible lead. Among 44 conditions with RI maple seedlings at least five feet long, 13 had recorded new saplings at follow-up; among 46 without such seedlings, 1 did. This is a retrospective association in an existing sample. It is not a held-out comparison with seedling abundance, proof of individual survival, or a management threshold.
The information constraint remains decisive: the existing later-year split would provide 10 development events and 4 assessment events. No height-class model is fitted. The current contribution is a reconciled measurement audit and a more specific testable hypothesis; evidence for an operational survey tool remains absent.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Endpoint and population
The source population is the 922 eligible intervals from the recruitment study, not all Michigan forest conditions. The outcome remains a new live sugar-maple sapling tally at follow-up, using the existing species, diameter, reconciliation, predecessor, and shared-sampling checks. No eligibility rule is relaxed to obtain more RI records or events.
Baseline RI is a potential predictor. Follow-up RI is a different measurement and is not needed to establish baseline length structure when the follow-up TREE endpoint is otherwise valid. Requiring RI at both visits would answer a narrower question and could discard valid baseline observations. Neither condition intervals nor sampled microplots are whole management stands, and these results are not statewide, survey-weighted population estimates.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Sampling and protocol definitions
The database dictionary retires REGEN_SUBP_STATUS_CD from inventory year 2015 and identifies REGEN_MICR_STATUS_CD as the status field populated across years. Code 1 identifies sampled RI on accessible forest; code 2 is sampled but without accessible forest on the microplot. Codes 3-5 are nonsampled and code 9 is historically ambiguous. A blank retired field is therefore not a reason to reject an otherwise valid code-1 forest sample. Conversely, code 2 cannot verify RI coverage of a positive forest-condition area. (Burrill et al. 2025, sec. 6.2.10 and 6.2.22)
The baseline screen requires RI plot presence, code-1 coverage of every contributing condition-microplot slice, consistent subplot identifiers, compatible core sampling, and a reconstructed condition area matching the existing microplot proportion. RI seedling records must have valid condition and subplot-condition foreign keys, species/source/length codes, and counts. Duplicate keys stop the calculation; invalid records make the affected plot’s RI measurements unavailable. Missing species tallies are not zero-filled until the measurement frame passes.
The inspected annual supplements specify a May-September RI window and established seedlings at least two inches long, below one inch DBH. Length is measured along the seedling from base to terminal bud, not necessarily vertical height. Counts above five may be estimated. Stump sprouts and suckers from one origin are not independent stems; only the tallest qualifying stump sprout is tallied. These details limit biological interpretations of the count totals. (U.S. Forest Service 2016, sec. 6.0 and 6.4; U.S. Forest Service 2018, 18–22)

The codes agree in the inspected 2016-2018 supplements and the v9.4 dictionary. Source code 1 denotes other seedlings and code 2 stump sprouts; code 3 is reserved for selected large-seeded species, not sugar maple. (U.S. Forest Service 2017, 21–22; Burrill et al. 2025, secs. 6.3.14–16)
The inspected supplements and the FIA dictionary define the length schema used here. They provide the documentary basis for this audit, but they do not substitute for a year-by-year review of every field supplement. (McWilliams et al. 2015, 18–23 and 72)

Historical coverage and date limitations
The full relevant sections of the 2016, 2017, and 2018 annual supplements were inspected. These years cover 37 available baseline intervals with four events. The 53 older intervals have dictionary and historical technical-report support, but their individual 2012-2015 annual supplements were not recovered. Full version-by-version protocol equivalence is not certified.
The official archive’s 2016 copy is marked DRAFT. Its length boundaries agree with the inspected 2017/2018 supplements and dictionary, but a final deployed 2016 edition is not certified. Older generic cross-references also retain inconsistent subplot/status wording; the audit uses the explicit microplot status table and dictionary. These qualifications are retained in the data dictionary and analysis decisions.
PLOT.MANUAL is not treated as a precise P2+ supplement edition: for example, baseline records store 7.0 while the available annual supplements include 7.1 and 7.2. Year-specific documentary coverage is recorded separately. Plot measurement dates provide a plausibility screen, not proof of the exact RI measurement day or leaf condition; the RI tables expose no separate field date.

title: Regeneration length classes and measurement feasibility
text:
Forecasting feasibility and next decision
A development/assessment split following the existing calendar boundary has 53 development intervals with ten events and 37 later intervals with four events, with no shared physical plots across the split. One missed assessment event would change observed event recall by 25 percentage points. These already explored outcomes are not an untouched validation set even if their length predictors were previously unused.
As a precision illustration only, even a hypothetical rule finding all 14 event plots would have an exact two-sided binomial 95% lower recall bound of 76.8% under independent-event sampling. This is not the observed rule’s recall, a clustered confidence interval, or a sample-size justification. Geographic dependence and a held-out sample would further constrain what can be learned.
The evidence supports retaining length structure as the next measurement hypothesis. It does not support a six-class fitted forecasting model or an operational score from this subset. A useful next study would fix a single supportable length representation, retain ordinary counts and sampling area as comparators on identical cases, and evaluate the paired gain in a separate, adequately supported inventory sample. A meaningful gain, forecasting horizon, decision target, action unit, and measurement cost must be specified first.
Within the existing Michigan snapshot, the baseline measurement milestone is complete with the historical-access qualifications above. The defensible contribution is the distinction between seedling abundance, length structure, and recorded sapling entry, together with explicit limits on usefulness. Acquiring other inventories or coordinating field work requires a separate scope decision; neither has occurred. The survey validation plan records these gates.
The subsequent count-versus-length design fixes a one-term comparison and planning scenarios. Its outcome-free historical opportunity screen finds only six physical plots beyond the current recruitment cohort among positive-seedling opportunities, before full eligibility checks. It does not establish a new independent Michigan test sample.

Here, a sapling has a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in diameter at breast height. A new recorded sapling is not an individually tracked baseline seedling. These sample results do not establish statewide regeneration rates, diagnose why entry was absent, or identify a forest treatment.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Abstract
I examined whether ordinary Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) seedling counts predict recorded sugar-maple (Acer saccharum) sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods and whether existing maple size structure improves prediction. The cohort contained 922 intervals on 903 physical plots across 66 counties, with baseline visits in 2011–2018 and follow-ups in 2018–2025; 169 new live saplings occurred in 100 conditions. I compared four prespecified logistic models using county-level cross-validation and 300 county-bootstrap resamples per population with model refitting. After accounting for sampled coverage and elapsed time, count-model AUC was 0.796 overall and 0.699 among 672 conditions with baseline seedlings. Counts improved Brier score relative to observation design alone, although the improvement among conditions with seedlings was uncertain. Adding maple sapling density and established-maple basal area changed Brier score by -0.00163 (95% interval -0.00529 to 0.00263) overall; the corresponding interval among conditions with seedlings also crossed zero. Separately, 1,580 comparable tagged saplings included 334 recorded deaths, 1,188 live saplings, and 58 live stems reaching 12.7 cm diameter. Seedling counts were informative about recorded entry, but the additional value of maple size structure was uncertain. These retrospective, unweighted comparisons do not establish regeneration adequacy or justify an operational management rule.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Study implications
Seedling counts were associated with new sugar-maple saplings recorded at the next inventory, but abundant seedlings do not establish successful replacement of canopy trees. In this Michigan sample, adding the abundance of existing maple saplings and larger maples did not clearly improve prediction over counts alone. Managers should distinguish recorded sapling entry from adequate regeneration and retain simple benchmarks when evaluating more elaborate indicators. The study does not identify a treatment, diagnose deer damage, or validate a rule for allocating field visits.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Introduction
Successful regeneration requires seedlings to advance into larger size classes. Michigan field studies describe plentiful small seedlings alongside limited larger regeneration (Henry et al. 2021). Sugar-maple age structure in managed northern hardwoods also shows that small-diameter stems may be old; existing saplings do not necessarily represent recent establishment (Henry and Walters 2023). These studies differ from standard FIA in their stand samples and size definitions, so their estimates cannot be treated as statewide rates for the cohort examined here.
Previous FIA research has examined the relationship between seedling measurements and subsequent recruitment. Harris and colleagues compared one seedling class with six height classes using boosted regression trees, including conspecific sapling abundance and tree basal area as candidate predictors. Their species-specific analyses were restricted to subplots with baseline seedlings, and taller seedlings were particularly informative (Harris et al. 2022). Their work provides a basis for evaluating the contribution of both seedling measurements and existing conspecific size classes. Recent northeastern studies distinguish small-seedling composition from established sapling abundance (Harris et al. 2026b) and examine recovery after disturbance over longer intervals (Harris et al. 2026a).
I examine how much information routinely available seedling counts provide about recorded sapling entry after accounting for sampled coverage and the time between inventories. I then test whether existing maple saplings and larger trees improve prediction on the same observations. This regional comparison complements earlier FIA studies while distinguishing recruitment from changes in the status of previously tagged saplings. Differences in subplot populations, seedling definitions, and validation procedures prevent direct comparison with published AUC values from studies using regeneration indicator (RI) measurements.
I set three primary objectives: quantify the predictive contribution of ordinary seedling counts, assess the additional contribution of maple sapling density and established-maple basal area, and describe the subsequent fates of tagged baseline saplings. I also evaluated fixed survey-selection strategies and examined the comparability of ordinary counts with RI length measurements. These secondary analyses address possible applications and measurement extensions of the main study.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Methods

Source and cohort
I used the pinned Michigan FIADB SQLite snapshot and current-evaluation cohort, EVALID 262501, rather than all historical intervals. Baseline ecological eligibility is accessible northern hardwood forest (type group 800) with live established sugar maple at least five inches diameter. The selected baseline forest-type codes are 801, 802, 805, and 809. Follow-up forest type need not remain in group 800. The source pair construction requires an intended plot predecessor, one-to-one condition mapping, at least 90% mapped-area overlap relative to both visits, and a 4.5–8.5-year interval. I document the selection and joins in the analysis decisions.
The recruitment audit additionally verifies sampled forest and mapped microplot-condition area at both visits. Both visits use the national design, the same offset microplot arrangement, and manual versions at least 5.1. I treated follow-ups as remeasurements and retained production QA codes 1 and 7. QA 7 is a supervised production check, not an invalid duplicate (Burrill et al. 2025).
Direct subplot predecessor identifiers (PREV_SBP_CN) are entirely unpopulated in this snapshot. I reconstructed continuity from the verified plot predecessor, subplot number, and microplot condition-change matrix. Nine source pairs failed the conservative matrix-versus-condition proportion check; one contains unresolved newly recorded saplings. I excluded these ten pairs rather than assigning zero outcomes. One separately verified sampled follow-up has no live TREE records and BALIVE=0; its missing derived tree metrics are reconciled to zero only in the new recruitment dataset.
The starting current-evaluation dataset contains 932 condition intervals. The nine inconsistent mappings and one ambiguous-entry interval are distinct exclusions, leaving 922. The 914 exact-overlap intervals and the 672 intervals with baseline seedlings are alternative subsets of that retained cohort, not additional sequential exclusions. Conditions represent mapped forest domains within a plot; a physical plot can therefore contribute more than one condition. The analytical unit is one condition observed across its two linked visits, not a seedling, individual microplot, or independent stand.
Eligible rows must have complete, finite outcomes and predictor fields. The modeling code stops on missing required values rather than silently dropping different rows for different models. I did not impute predictors. I set absent species tallies to zero only after sampled-forest eligibility and record checks; I did not assign zero to an unsampled or ambiguous interval.


Recorded recruitment endpoint
The binary response is at least one new live sugar-maple sapling at follow-up: SPCD=318, STATUSCD=1, diameter at least one and less than five inches (2.54 to less than 12.7 cm), RECONCILECD=1, and no predecessor TREE record. Candidates must occur on a comparable shared sampled microplot. Reconcile code 1 can also describe entry on formerly nonforest land, so it is insufficient without the preceding sampling-frame checks (Burrill et al. 2025).
These are recorded surviving entrants into the FIA sapling class, not individual baseline seedlings followed through time. Entrants that die before remeasurement or exceed the restricted size class are not counted. Large newly recorded subplot trees are excluded because sampled area increases at the five-inch boundary. Exact mapped-area overlap is a sensitivity analysis; mapped fractions do not establish an individual stem’s lineage or exact location.


Predictors and fixed comparisons
I treated all eligible pairs and the subset with baseline seedlings detected as principal analysis populations and fit models separately. The second population asks whether measurements distinguish entrants among conditions already containing seedlings. Both use four fixed logistic models:

Training-sample prevalence only.
Observation design: baseline microplot coverage and realized interval.
Count and design: those variables plus log1p ordinary maple seedling count.
Stages and design: the count model plus log1p baseline maple sapling density and log1p established-maple basal area.

Ordinary counts sum SEEDLING.TREECOUNT and are checked against TREECOUNT_CALC. Sapling density uses FIA stem expansion and sampled microplot area; established-maple basal area uses live stems at least five inches diameter and the corresponding sampled area. Coverage is a model covariate, not a claim that raw counts were collected over identical footprints. Standard hardwood tallies omit the smallest seedlings, and counts above five may be estimated (U.S. Forest Service 2023). A recorded count is not necessarily an exact number of independent seed-origin individuals.
Training-only standardization precedes fitting. The objective is summed binomial negative log likelihood plus \(\lambda\sum_j\beta_j^2/2\) for slopes, with \(\lambda=1\) and an unpenalized intercept. This fixed ridge penalty was not tuned to optimize the findings. Ordinary GLM coefficient p-values are not attached to penalized fits. No additional competitor, beech, climate, or treatment predictor is selected after examining these recruitment results.

I transformed each predictor before centering and dividing by its training-sample standard deviation. I applied the same training center and scale to held-out observations. I used a scale of one for a constant training predictor to prevent division by zero. The model is \(p_i=1/(1+\exp(-\eta_i))\), where \(\eta_i=\beta_0+\sum_j\beta_j z_{ij}\) and the included standardized predictors follow the four-model sequence. Coverage and interval enter as estimated slopes, not offsets. The response is binary entry, so the model does not estimate the number of new saplings or an annual recruitment rate.
The production optimizer uses Newton steps with a backtracking line search, a maximum of 100 iterations, and finite-coefficient and gradient checks. Model dimensions are zero, two, three, and five slopes, respectively, plus the intercept. Coefficients from subsequent fits to each complete analysis population are descriptive summaries; all performance claims use held-out predictions, not those full-population fitted values. The appendix reports the coefficients without unpenalized standard errors or significance stars.


Validation and uncertainty
Five folds hold out entire counties, balancing condition counts without using outcomes in assignment. All models within a population use identical observations and folds. Every physical plot stays in one fold. Scaling and fitting use training counties only. County separation prevents the same county from entering both sets, but does not impose a distance buffer between nearby plots in neighboring counties or guarantee environmental separation.
Brier score and log loss evaluate probabilities; AUC and average precision (AP) evaluate discrimination. Losses average equally over condition intervals: they are neither plot-balanced nor FIA survey-weighted population estimates. I estimated calibration intercept and slope jointly by regressing outcomes on held-out log odds. These are diagnostics, not recalibration of predictions; the joint intercept is not a separately fitted calibration-in-the-large intercept. Mean predicted probability and the observed-to-expected ratio are also exported. Rank metrics for the prevalence benchmark are omitted because differences in fold-specific prevalence do not constitute a meaningful individual ranking.
Specifically, the Brier score is the mean squared probability error, \(n^{-1}\sum_i(y_i-p_i)^2\). Log loss is \(-n^{-1}\sum_i[y_i\log(p_i)+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]\); probabilities are bounded between \(10^{-12}\) and \(1-10^{-12}\) for numerical scoring. Lower losses are better. AUC compares event and nonevent rankings with half credit for tied probabilities. AP sums precision over increments in recall after grouping equal probabilities. AP depends on event prevalence, so the two nested populations are not interchangeable benchmarks. I report probability loss, ranking, and calibration separately because improvement in one need not imply improvement in the others.
I ordered counties by descending condition count, used county identifier to break ties, and assigned each county to the currently least-loaded fold. Fold size, then county count, then fold number resolve assignment ties. This is a single deterministic partition, not repeated random cross-validation. The two populations receive their own size-balanced partition. Metrics pool all out-of-fold predictions within each population rather than averaging its five fold-specific AUC values. Appendix fold denominators show how many events actually support each held-out comparison.
I used 300 resamples per population of whole counties, repeating scaling and all held-out fits. All 600 resamples succeed. Original fold assignments, model set, and penalty remain fixed. Paired differences subtract the reference model on identical cases; negative Brier differences favor the added information. Percentile intervals characterize this resampling scheme. They exclude uncertainty from selecting the question, cohort, model set, and source snapshot. These data were already explored; this is not preregistration or external validation. The 300 draws provide finite Monte Carlo precision for the interval endpoints; their displayed digits should not be read as equally precise inferential information. No equivalence margin or minimum useful improvement was specified, and no multiple-comparison correction is applied. Interpretation emphasizes the matched Brier contrasts; additional metrics and secondary analyses are descriptive.
Each bootstrap draw samples the population’s counties with replacement, using the same number of county draws as observed counties. Every condition in a selected county receives its county’s sampling multiplicity as a frequency weight. All copies remain in that county’s original fold, so resampling cannot put a duplicate county into both training and testing. Weighted training means, sample standard deviations, model fits, and pooled scores are recomputed in each draw. Counties drawn zero times have no evaluation weight. The reported limits are the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 300 resulting metrics or paired differences, not standard errors calculated by treating 922 conditions as independent replicates. The stored seed is 20260908 in each population; this does not make the nested analyses independent.
Descriptive count-bin intervals use a separate 2,000-draw county resampling of observed event fractions, without fitting a model. A bin with no observed events has a degenerate empirical interval at zero; it does not establish a zero population risk. These intervals and the model-refit intervals answer different questions and should not be combined.
Fixed sensitivities restrict to exact overlap or follow-up manual version at least 9, or use penalties 0 and 4. A retrospective temporal assessment trains on follow-ups before 2023 and tests 2023 onward, with no shared physical plots. Realized interval is known at follow-up. Accordingly, these are conditional next-visit assessments, not validated fixed-horizon forecasts available at baseline. Count agreement and manual-version screening do not establish that every historical field procedure is identical; individual baseline regional editions were not all verified.


Linked sapling fates
A companion cohort follows live tagged baseline maple saplings on the expected successor plot before restricting follow-up species, status, or diameter. Comparable recorded death, live persistence below five inches, and live advancement to at least five inches are separated from frame inconsistency, species reidentification, and no-longer-sampled records. I assessed fate eligibility separately from the new-entrant outcome: an ambiguous new arrival does not alone invalidate an existing tagged stem’s link. I calculated annual diameter difference as follow-up minus baseline diameter divided by elapsed years and summarized it only for comparable surviving maples. No mortality mechanism, treatment effect, or independent-stem sampling assumption is imposed.


Use of AI assistance
I used OpenAI Codex to assist with literature searching, analysis-code development and checking, and manuscript revision. Computational checks do not constitute independent scientific review. I retain responsibility for the data interpretation, references, and submitted content.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Discussion
Ordinary seedling counts contain information about recorded sapling entry in this selected Michigan sample. The count gradient and pooled probability-loss improvement argue against dismissing standard tallies as uninformative. However, discrimination is weaker within baseline detections, and its paired Brier improvement is uncertain. Abundant seedlings therefore indicate a higher chance of observing entry without establishing a secure advancing cohort.
The added maple-stage predictors produce only small, uncertain improvements over a strong count benchmark. They do not improve captured entrants at the tested equal capacity, and their survey-priority point gain over raw counts is not reproduced in the later-year comparison. These are substantive limits of the tested predictors and models, not reasons to continue adding variables until a preferred explanation appears. Uncertainty spanning zero is not proof of no effect, practical equivalence, or irrelevance under every model form.
In particular, existing sapling density and larger-tree basal area do not measure the height distribution of seedlings approaching the sapling boundary. Their uncertain incremental value therefore does not contradict evidence for height-resolved inventories (Harris et al. 2022). The additive, transformed linear predictors also leave nonlinear responses and interactions untested. The results limit the specific benchmark models evaluated here, not all possible uses of stage structure.
The fate analysis explains why size-class absence and mortality must remain distinct. Surviving stems can move beyond the sapling boundary, while species reidentification and sampling corrections also alter apparent stage membership. Conversely, a new live sapling at one revisit does not measure all arrivals during the interval, adequate stocking, genetic origin, or subsequent survival to the canopy. Neither record-based endpoint supports a causal claim about browsing, competitors, or management.

Scope and limitations
The target is retained sampled conditions, not all Michigan forests. Baseline ecological selection, current-evaluation membership, accessible forest, remeasurement, comparable area, and unambiguous records restrict inclusion. The exclusion audit protects outcome interpretation but does not remove selection bias. County grouping addresses part of the dependence structure; it does not provide survey weights or independent experimental replication. The main scores give each condition interval equal weight, so plots contributing more than one condition receive more total evaluation weight.
Finite event support, estimated seedling tallies, varying sampled area and exposure duration, model-form choices, incomplete historical manual review, and one fixed source snapshot limit generalization. Resampling does not correct all of these limitations. Near-matching mean predicted and observed event fractions is not evidence of calibration everywhere, and the retrospective temporal split is not an untouched external test.
The two analysis populations are nested and do not provide independent replications. Observed entry combines growth into the defined diameter class, survival until remeasurement, and recording on a small sampled footprint. Zero recorded entry cannot distinguish slow growth from mortality or absence of suitable seedlings. Likewise, the tagged-stem fate sample does not follow the untagged baseline seedlings; it cannot decompose their failure to enter the sapling class. Unmeasured browsing, understory competition, and disturbance may influence these processes, but this analysis does not estimate their effects.


Implications and optional future work
The practical implication is to retain simple count-based benchmarks and state precisely what they predict. A management tool would additionally require a defined action, independently assessed survey need or treatment response, consequences of errors, and relevant external evaluation. No operational ranking or intervention rule is released.
Length structure is a plausible follow-on hypothesis motivated by earlier FIA work (Harris et al. 2022), not the unfulfilled central objective of this paper. A separate design specifies a matched count-versus-length comparison and evaluation safeguards. Regional inventory acquisition and field validation are deferred extensions. Wisconsin or Minnesota data are not required to complete the bounded Michigan results, and no regional outcome or height-model result is claimed.

title: Ordinary seedling counts and recorded sugar maple sapling recruitment in Michigan northern hardwoods
text:
Conclusion
Standard FIA seedling counts provide limited information about next-visit recorded sugar-maple sapling entry in selected Michigan northern hardwood conditions. Existing maple sapling density and established-maple basal area show no clear incremental improvement over the count benchmark under the specified comparisons. Linked tagged-stem accounting separately identifies recorded death, persistent live saplings, and surviving advancement beyond the sapling class. The core finding is an evidence-based boundary on what these common observations establish—not a claim of regeneration adequacy, biological failure, or validated management usefulness.

A forest can contain many seedlings without those seedlings becoming the next generation of larger trees. This study compares repeated public USDA Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) observations in Michigan to ask what early maple counts tell us about new saplings recorded several years later.

Here, a sapling is a tree with a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in diameter at breast height. It is not a mature canopy tree.

title: Canopy to Cohort
text:
Three findings to take away

More seedlings were a useful clue, not a guarantee
Conditions with higher starting counts more often had new maple saplings at the next visit. But even among the 280 conditions with more than 20 seedlings recorded initially, only 72 (25.7%) had a qualifying new sapling recorded later. Seedling abundance alone does not establish that the future forest is secure.



New saplings were recorded more often where the starting seedling count was higher. Bars show the percentage of sampled forest conditions with entry; vertical lines show county-resampling uncertainty. The zero-count group’s zero-width interval reflects no observed events, not proof that entry is impossible.




Adding more maple measurements did not clearly improve prediction
The study compared models on the same observations, testing each on counties excluded from its training data. Adding the abundance of existing maple saplings and larger maples produced small improvements in probability error, but the uncertainty included both improvement and worsening. These results do not yet show a dependable advantage over the simpler seedling-count model.
The models account for the area sampled and the time between visits. They are retrospective comparisons, not a validated tool for prescribing forest treatment.


Leaving the sapling size class does not always mean dying
A separate check followed 1,580 comparable, previously tagged maple saplings: 1,188 remained live saplings, 334 were recorded dead, and 58 remained alive after growing to at least 5 inches in trunk diameter. Keeping these outcomes separate prevents healthy growth from being mistaken for loss.

title: Canopy to Cohort
section: What this means for forest assessment
text:
What this means for forest assessment
Seedling counts are worth measuring, but they are one part of the picture. Repeated visits help distinguish new sapling entry, continued survival, growth into a larger size class, and recorded death.
No new sapling recorded does not by itself mean regeneration has failed. The inventory samples small areas, seedlings are not individually tagged, and some entrants may die or grow beyond the studied size class between visits. These are unweighted results for the study sample, not statewide rates.

What starting seedling counts tell us
Conditions with more recorded seedlings at baseline more often contained a new live maple sapling at the next visit. Among the 280 conditions with more than 20 starting seedlings, 72 (25.7%) had a qualifying new sapling. The remaining conditions had no qualifying recorded entry on the sampled area.

Vertical lines show uncertainty from resampling whole counties. A group with no observed events has a zero-width empirical interval; it does not establish zero population probability.





A qualifying sapling has a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in diameter at breast height. The inventory does not individually link each baseline seedling to a later sapling. These observations therefore show recorded entry without establishing adequate replacement of canopy trees.

section: Do additional maple measurements improve prediction?
text:
Do additional maple measurements improve prediction?
I compared models on identical observations and tested them on counties excluded from training. The first comparison adds seedling count to sampling coverage and elapsed time. The second adds existing maple sapling density and established-maple basal area to that count model.
The horizontal axis shows the change in average probability error, measured by the Brier score. Values to the left of zero favor the added measurements. The horizontal lines show 95% intervals from resampling counties and refitting the models. An interval crossing zero includes both improvement and worsening.








Figure 3: Change in Brier score when measurements are added to the model. Negative differences indicate lower probability error. The two panels evaluate all eligible observations and the subset with starting seedlings. The subsets overlap and do not provide independent replications.





Counts improved average probability error across all eligible observations. Within the subset that already contained seedlings, the Brier improvement was less certain. Adding maple size measurements produced small point improvements, with intervals crossing zero in both populations. These comparisons did not establish a dependable predictive advantage from the additional size measurements.
The full results also report calibration, other performance measures, sensitivity checks, and the fates of tagged saplings.

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
This optional follow-up design builds on the completed Michigan recruitment study. It specifies the additional measurements and evaluation sample needed to assess seedling length. Regional acquisition and external validation are future work.
Determine whether the length distribution of established sugar-maple seedlings improves predictions of recorded sapling entry beyond ordinary seedling counts on the same sampled area. The immediate scientific product is a paired measurement comparison with a credible assessment sample. A survey-ranking tool, a treatment prescription, and a forecast of canopy replacement are different products requiring additional evidence.
The Michigan measurement audit supplies local feasibility evidence: 90 baseline intervals on 87 physical plots contain 14 recruit-bearing conditions. The 71 intervals with ordinary baseline seedling detections contain all 14 events. Taller-seedling presence is associated with subsequent entry, but its added value after accounting for abundance has not been estimated. The current later-year partition supplies only four assessment events.
Regional research already compared ordinary counts with six RI length classes and found that taller seedlings were important predictors. The proposed one-term comparison is therefore a parsimonious regional assessment, not the discovery that height matters or an exact replication of the published boosted tree models. (Harris et al. 2022)

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
Primary population and endpoint
The primary comparison is among conditions with ordinary baseline sugar-maple seedlings, not the easier mixture of detected and undetected seedlings. Retain the northern-hardwood/adult-maple scope and verified common sampling opportunity from the recruitment study. A regional extension must use harmonized definitions and report each geography separately; a result outside Michigan is a transport assessment, not independent validation of Michigan-specific performance.
The outcome remains at least one new live sugar-maple sapling recorded at the next visit: species 318, live status, diameter at least one and below five inches, reconciliation code 1, no predecessor TREE identifier, and the audited common microplot frame. It excludes ambiguous procedure changes and missed-tree tallies. It is not an individual seedling conversion rate: intervening entrants that die before remeasurement are not observed.
Apply the existing baseline RI frame and count checks before assigning any tally zero. Preserve invalid or inaccessible observations as unavailable. Historical manual access remains qualified, including the 2016 archived draft and the unrecovered 2012-2015 annual supplements. A broader cohort needs its own year-specific review rather than inheriting blanket approval from the 90 cases.

Let N denote the ordinary baseline maple count, H the RI count in classes 5-6 (at least five feet long), A the sampled microplot coverage, and T the elapsed interval. The proposed length feature is Q = H/N. It is undefined when N is zero; those conditions are outside the primary comparison, not assigned Q = 0.

Both models use identical cases and development-only standardization. Do not add beech, browse score, six separate classes, interactions, alternative cutoffs, or a favorable model family after inspecting evaluation results. This choice limits the question to one candidate length representation; a negative result would not prove that no length-based method could help.
A required, predeclared sensitivity replaces the single log-count slope with a three-degree-of-freedom natural spline of log(1 + N) in both models, while retaining A, T, and the same single Q addition. Set knots and boundary knots from development data only, standardize the resulting basis there, and use the same fixed ridge penalty. This gives five versus six slopes and must be included in development-support planning. Report it alongside the primary linear-log-count comparison, not as a replacement chosen after seeing results. If the length gain disappears against flexible counts, limit the conclusion to the original model forms; do not claim established added measurement value.
Ordinary counts must be reconciled with RI classes 3-6 on the same sampled area. Unresolved differences stop the comparison before fitting: silently retaining only agreements could create a selected sample. RI seedlings below one foot are excluded from N and Q. Their potential information is a separate question and is not mixed into this one-term length comparison.
For each physical plot, choose the latest completed eligible visit interval within the declared development or assessment period using dates and protocol eligibility, not outcome values. Retain eligible conditions from that interval. Keep every visit and condition of a physical plot on the same side of the development/assessment boundary. Give each plot total training weight one, divided across its included conditions. Freeze this interval-selection and weighting rule before any new outcome comparison.

title: Count-versus-length study design
section: Timing and the claim being tested
text:
Timing and the claim being tested
The primary estimand is a retrospective next-visit probability comparison conditional on the realized interval within 4.5-8.5 years. Realized T is shared by both models, so the comparison can test added length information after adjusting for observation duration. However, the actual next-visit date is not known at baseline. This estimand is not an operational forecast made at baseline.
A future forecast must instead specify a genuinely planned horizon and collect or identify outcomes at that horizon. Merely setting T = 7 when scoring existing variable-duration outcomes does not validate seven-year risks. There is no observed exact crossing date from which to reconstruct an exact seven-year recruitment event. The current study should retain the narrower conditional claim until suitable timing evidence exists.

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
Evaluation and meaningful improvement
The primary metric is paired Brier gain: count-model squared probability error minus length-model squared error. Average the condition-level differences within each physical plot, then average across plots:
\[
D_j = \frac{1}{m_j}\sum_{i=1}^{m_j}
\left[(y_{ij}-p_{0,ij})^2-(y_{ij}-p_{1,ij})^2\right],
\qquad \Delta = \frac{1}{J}\sum_{j=1}^{J}D_j.
\]
Positive gain favors length. Equal plot weighting prevents plots with more conditions from automatically dominating the evaluation. It differs from a condition-average estimator, which must not be substituted as the benchmark. This is a selected-cohort comparison, not a statewide design-weighted estimate of forest condition.
Evaluate the frozen models once on the reserved sample. Resample whole counties for paired uncertainty, retaining all selected plot/condition records within each county. Such evaluation intervals are conditional on the frozen training fits; they do not include every source of model-development uncertainty. Report geographic event support, calibration curves/intercept/slope, and discrimination alongside Brier gain. With too few independent county clusters, a nominal bootstrap interval is not a sufficient precision guarantee.
A lower confidence limit above zero supports a statistical improvement for these models and this target. To claim a meaningful improvement, first declare a minimum gain delta and require the lower limit to exceed it. An interval spanning zero is inconclusive, not proof of equivalence. Neither an arbitrary Brier threshold nor a small P value supplies field utility. The necessary measurement costs and error consequences remain unspecified.

title: Count-versus-length study design
text:
Precision scenarios
External-assessment sample sizes depend on the target population, anticipated predictions, calibration, and desired precision; an event-count rule alone cannot establish adequacy. The published guidance concerns clinical models; its design principles transfer, but its clinical thresholds and numerical examples are not forestry sample-size recommendations. (Riley et al. 2024)
The following calculation is a transparent planning approximation for the mean of frozen plot-level paired losses. With assumed SD s, variance inflation V, and target 95% interval half-width h, use
\[
J_{\mathrm{complete}} = \left\lceil V(1.96s/h)^2\right\rceil.
\]
The implementation uses the exact normal quantile rather than rounded 1.96. Candidate plot numbers are complete plots divided by an assumed retention fraction, rounded upward. This scales expected yield; it does not guarantee the required number will be retained, remove attrition bias, or certify power.

title: Analysis decisions
text: I used repeated public FIA observations to evaluate three questions: how much ordinary seedling counts tell us about recorded sapling entry, whether maple size structure adds predictive information, and what happens to tagged baseline saplings. This page documents the decisions behind the research paper.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Source and cohort
I used the Michigan FIADB SQLite snapshot identified in configuration and the provenance audit. The source archive has SHA-256 2c1eb908a47436d4edd0f3ba9e3d647b79a4f36cef972c5ba83277300817aee1.
Evaluation 262501 supplies the current-evaluation cohort. I selected baseline accessible forests in maple/beech/birch group 800 with live sugar maple at least five inches in diameter. The selected forest-type codes are 801, 802, 805, and 809; sugar maple is SPCD=318. Follow-up forest type may change.
I required an intended plot predecessor, one-to-one condition mapping, at least 90% mapped microplot-area overlap relative to each visit, and an interval of 4.5–8.5 years. A forest condition is a mapped part of a plot with similar forest characteristics. One plot can contribute more than one condition.
The source contains 932 condition pairs. Nine fail the conservative shared-area check and one contains ambiguous new saplings. Excluding these leaves 922 intervals on 903 physical plots in 66 counties. The cohort flow records these counts and the alternative restrictions. Baseline measurements span 2011–2018 and follow-ups span 2018–2025.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Sampling and linkage checks
Both visits must use the national design, an unchanged microplot arrangement, manual version at least 5.1, and demonstrated sampled forest. Follow-ups must be remeasurements. I retained production QA codes 1 and 7; code 7 identifies a supervised production check.
The direct subplot predecessor field, PREV_SBP_CN, is empty in this snapshot. I reconstructed continuity from the verified plot predecessor, subplot number, and SUBP_COND_CHNG_MTRX microplot links. The mapped shared proportion cannot exceed the corresponding condition proportion at either visit. Any populated predecessor identifier must agree with its expected link.
The frame audit and protocol audit record these checks. The 914 exact-overlap intervals form a sensitivity subset.
I assigned zero only after establishing sampling opportunity and verifying the relevant records. One fully checked follow-up with no live TREE records and BALIVE=0 has an explicit zero correction. The model code stops on missing required predictors; it does not impute them or silently change the observations across models.

title: Analysis decisions
Analysis decisions
text:
Predictors and model comparisons
I fit the same four logistic benchmarks separately to all 922 eligible intervals and the 672 intervals with baseline seedlings. The second population tests whether measurements distinguish entry among conditions that already contained seedlings. Both populations contain the same 100 conditions with recorded entry and overlap rather than providing independent replications.







Model
Predictors




Prevalence
Training-sample event fraction


Observation design
Baseline microplot coverage and elapsed interval


Count and design
Observation design plus ordinary maple seedling count


Maple stages and design
Count and design plus maple sapling density and established-maple basal area



The ordinary count sums SEEDLING.TREECOUNT; the audit checks agreement with TREECOUNT_CALC. Sapling density accounts for microplot condition coverage. Established-maple basal area uses live stems at least five inches in diameter and the appropriate sampled area.
I apply log(1 + x) to count, sapling density, and basal area. Centering and scaling use training data only and repeat within each bootstrap fit. The ridge objective is summed binomial negative log likelihood plus one-half the sum of squared slopes. The intercept is unpenalized and the primary penalty is fixed at one. I did not tune it to improve these findings.
The data dictionary lists the source fields and units. The model module implements these comparisons.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Validation and uncertainty
I held out whole counties in five folds. Assignment balances condition counts without using outcomes, and every physical plot stays in one fold. Each population has its own deterministic partition. All models within a population use identical observations and folds.
Brier score and log loss evaluate probability error; AUC and average precision evaluate ranking. The scores give equal weight to condition intervals. They are unweighted sample summaries. Joint calibration intercept and slope, mean predicted probability, and observed-to-expected ratios describe calibration.
Paired uncertainty uses 300 resamples of whole counties per population. Each draw repeats training scaling and model fitting while preserving the county folds, model set, and penalty. All 600 draws succeeded. Negative model-minus-reference Brier differences favor the added information. Separate descriptive count-bin intervals use 2,000 county resamples.
I had explored this source snapshot before fixing the recruitment comparisons. The analysis is retrospective, and its bootstrap does not include uncertainty from choosing the question, cohort, or model set. It does not provide external validation. I specified no equivalence margin or minimum useful improvement and applied no multiple-comparison correction.
See the validation results and paired differences.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Sensitivity and temporal comparisons
The fixed checks restrict observations to exact overlap or follow-up manual version at least 9, or change the penalty to 0 or 4. Each comparison uses matched observations. The sensitivity table reports the resulting denominators and scores.
The retrospective temporal comparison trains on follow-ups before 2023 and tests follow-ups from 2023 onward. No physical plot crosses that split, although counties can recur. Protocol and sample composition also change across years.
Elapsed interval is known at follow-up. These comparisons assess conditional next-visit outcomes over variable durations; they do not validate a fixed forecast horizon available at baseline.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Linked sapling fates
I linked tagged baseline maple saplings to TREE records on their expected successor plot before screening follow-up species, status, or diameter. Fate eligibility has its own checks: an ambiguous new entrant does not alone invalidate an existing stem’s link.
Of 1,593 baseline saplings, 1,580 have comparable biological fates: 334 recorded dead, 1,188 alive within the sapling class, and 58 alive at or above five inches. Nine stems fail frame consistency, three have a species reidentification, and one has a no-longer-sampled reconciliation. These 13 remain in the accounting without biological outcome assignments.
Annual diameter difference divides follow-up minus baseline diameter by elapsed years for comparable surviving maples. Recorded death and size-class advancement describe distinct outcomes. The study does not estimate a mortality mechanism or infer canopy replacement from growth beyond five inches.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Supporting analyses
The survey comparison evaluates fixed selection rules on the same observations. Its primary comparison integrates ties at 25% condition capacity; 10% and 50% are fixed alternatives. The target of no recorded entry does not independently establish survey need, field cost, or treatment benefit.
The RI measurement audit checks sampling coverage, dates, record codes, and seedling lengths in a subset of 90 intervals with 14 recorded-entry conditions. Ordinary counts match the RI counts at least one foot long on all 311 comparable microplot-condition intervals. The audit retains length classes and source categories. It does not fit a length model.

title: Analysis decisions
text:
Geography and interpretation
The study map joins FIA county identifiers to county polygons and displays counts of eligible condition intervals. Exact FIA plot coordinates are neither used nor inferred. Map colors show sample support and cannot establish county regeneration rates or rankings.
The results apply to the selected Michigan sample. They do not provide FIA survey-weighted statewide estimates, identify causes of absent entry, or validate a forest treatment. Adding maple size measurements did not clearly improve prediction under the specified comparisons; uncertainty spanning zero does not establish equivalence.
The reproducibility guide describes the pinned inputs, computation, and verification commands.
